newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: AN 80 MILLION DOLLAR FLUTTER ON THE CUP
More than A$80 million is likely to be wagered Australia-wide
on today's Melbourne Cup.
TAB spokeswoman Jill Hollingworth, says last year more money was bet on the Cup than ever before.
The TAB has put on more than one-thousand Tele-bet operators to
answer the quarter of a million calls expected... that compares to
around 140,000 on any normal Saturday.
Meanwhile the official rating for Flemington is good, with a Penetrometre reading of 4.46.
15.4 millimetres of rain fell on Sunday and course
manager Ross Bradfield will add three millimetres of watering this
morning.
SEARCH CONTINUES FOR ELDERLY WOMAN
In the foothills of the Victorian Alps, 30 volunteers are
searching for an elderly English woman who went for a walk last
night and did not come home.
The 69 year old woman was staying at a caravan park at
Harrietville, near Bright.
Twenty police, fire brigade members and State Emergency Service volunteers searched through the night with torches.
Senior Sergeant Rob Webb, says reinforcements have come from
Wangaratta, Benalla and Yackandandah.
He says the woman was not well equipped for a night in the cold.
CALLS FOR SACKING AFTER JUDGE SUICIDES
The New South Wales Opposition has called for the immediate sacking
of Upper House MP Franca Arena, following the suicide of a former
Supreme Court judge.
Justice David Yeldham was found dead in his car at his home in Sydney's north yesterday afternoon.
Justice Yeldham was one of two people named by Labor MLC Franca
Arena in New South Wales Parliament last week.
Under parliamentary privilege, she questioned whether he and former
south coast politician Frank Arkell had received preferential
treatment from the Police Royal Commission's paedophile investigators.
Justice Yeldham denied the allegations.
OSCAR SCHINDLER THE CUP FAVOURITE
Firstly to the Melbourne Cup.....and Irish import, Oscar Schindler,
is an easing favorite for today's big race. The big chestnut was heavily backed at odds of five-to-one, at
yesterday's Call of The Card.
Last year's winner, Doriemus, and The Bandette, also attracted big
wagers, with one punter laying 130-thousand dollars on the reigning
champion.
Meanwhile early arrivals at Flemington this morning will be confronted by cool and blustery conditions...and a heavy contingent
of security guards to ensure Cup revellry doesn't get out of hand.
CPSU LAUNCHES INDUSTRIAL CAMPAIGN
Industrial action will affect services to the public today in DSS
and CES offices in South Australia, New South Wales and the Members of the Public Sector Union are placing a half-day ban on
public contact, in protest against government plans to abolish the
CES and establish a new social security payment agency.
The union says the action this morning, affecting over-the-counter and phone contact, marks the start of rolling industrial action.
It'll affect other States and territories over the next week.
The union's South Australian secretary, Margaret Sexton, says it's
being taken because Federal ministers won't guarantee the future of
CES and DSS services and staff.
NEW DEVELOPMENT IN QLD'S CARRUTHERS SAGA
The Queensland QC whose resignation prompted a failed vote of no
confidence in the Borbidge Government, has ruled out any
chance of returning to complete his report for the Criminal Justice
Commission. Kenneth Carruthers resigned last week leaving his inquiries into
deals between the Government and the Police Union and the Labor
Party and the Sporting Shooters Association unfinished.
In a statement issued last night, Mr Carruthers says although he
was willing to return after seeing a copy of draft legislation proposed by the Opposition, the Government's attitude had since
made it impossible.
He says he thought his return had been desired by the government.
However, he says, he has been informed that the government has said
publicly that he should not return, and that the Bill doesn't have the support of the whole of the Queensland Parliament.
MEETING TODAY OVER MINING AT KAKADU
Aborigines, miners and government officials will meet in Kakadu
National Park today as part of an important study on the impact of
development on traditional aboriginal owners. The social study, which was demanded by aboriginal leaders, could
determine whether a future uranium mine goes ahead inside the
world-heritage listed park.
The study is being conducted independently from an environmental
impact study into the feasibility of a new uranium mine at the rich Jabiluka deposit.
But with senior traditional owners opposed to any new mine, the
results of a social impact study are considered critical.
CONCERNS OVER WORLD HERITAGE AREAS
An inquiry into the management of World Heritage Areas has found most of Australia's 11-sites are underfunded.
It's also recommending the introduction of a user-pays system and
sponsorship to help raise the A$20 million needed to correct
that situation.
Federal Parliament's Environment Committee has also found funding is inequitable, and there's an urgent need for funding arrangements
between the Commonwealth and the Queensland, New South Wales, South
Australian and West Australian Governments to be finalised.
Among the World Heritage Areas recognised as needing greaterfunding
are Fraser Island and Shark Bay.
MORE CALLS FOR INTEREST RATE CUT
The Australian Business Chamber says the Reserve Bank must cut
interest rates at its board meeting today.
Failure to do so, it says, would be an "opportunity disastrously
missed". The Chamber's Managing Director, Phillip Holt, says a cut in
interest rates would do more than anything else to revive business
and consumer confidence.
CU WELCOMES DROUGHT DECISION
The Cattlemen's Union has welcomed the Federal Government's announcement to extend drought recovery assistance.
Executive Director, Ruth Wade, says the A$81.5 million
package, which includes 10-million for herd rebuilding and pasture
re-establishment, provides hope for drought affected producers.
She says the extension of assistance will allow families to
continue to live and survive while they focus on getting their businesses back on track.
SURVIVING BLACKHAWK PILOT GIVES EVIDENCE
The Blackhawk inquiry has heard the pilot of Blackhawk Two didn't
give up control of his craft once it lost its tail rotor, knowing
the way the craft landed was a matter of survival.
The Military Board Inquiry into the mid air collision which killed
18 soldiers has heard the statement of Captain David Bourke, who
said he heard a crunch, an explosion then his aircraft began to
spin violently.
The inquiry was told he didn't give up control which was limited, but kept scanning for the horizon.
He became award of a sudden increase of light and as they spun to
the ground he realised they were basically upright, just before
impact he tried to level out.
DILI PHOTOS TO BE SHOWN IN EXHIBITION
Federal Labor frontbencher Laurie Ferguson has criticised
Parliament's decision to consult the Department of Foreign Affairs
and Trade over the contents of a photographic exhibition.
Federal Parliament won't allow photographs of the 1991 Dili
massacre in East Timor and other atrocities to be shown in a
planned exhibition of World War Two photographs. Mr Ferguson says he accepts the decision, because he inadvertently
failed to mention in the application the presence of post World War
Two East Timor photos.
But Mr Ferguson, who's the convenor of Parliamentarians for East
Timor, says Parliament should decide what is exhibited and why. He says the involvement of the Department leaves open the inference
that the decision may have been dictated by politics and the need
to keep Indonesia on side.
